title: A Hidden Bird Species, Revealed by DNA
hook: Two birds in Japan look nearly identical — but their DNA and songs say they're different species. The split is Japan's first new bird in 40 years, and shows how genetics keeps finding hidden life.
key_points: A bird long thought to be one rare species turned out to be two.
The newly named Tokara Leaf Warbler looks almost identical to Ijima's Leaf Warbler.
DNA and song — not appearance — revealed they are distinct species.
It's Japan's first new bird species discovery in more than 40 years.
Such look-alike 'cryptic species' show how much biodiversity hides in plain sight.
content_html: For decades, an elusive warbler in Japan was filed away as a single rare species. New work reported via ScienceDaily shows it was actually two. Alongside the known Ijima's Leaf Warbler lives a separate, newly identified Tokara Leaf Warbler — and to the eye, they look almost the same.
extra_html: What gave the secret away wasn't appearance but DNA and song. Genetic analysis showed the two populations were distinct, and their different songs — which birds use to attract mates of their own kind — back up the split. Look-alikes like these are called cryptic species: organisms so similar in form that they pass as one until molecular tools pull them apart. The discovery is Japan's first new bird species in more than 40 years, and a reminder of a larger pattern in biology. As DNA sequencing becomes routine, biologists keep finding that single "species" are really several, quietly revealing how much of life's diversity has been hiding in plain sight.

related.title: How Species Are Named
related.hook: Every species on Earth gets a two-word Latin name — like Homo sapiens — under a tidy ranked system invented 250 years ago that scientists still use today.

related.title: How New Species Form
related.hook: Split one population in two, let them drift apart long enough, and eventually they can no longer interbreed — that's speciation, the engine that fills the tree of life with branches.

flashcards.prompt: How did scientists show the two warblers are separate species?

choices.text: By their DNA and songs, despite near-identical appearances
By their dramatically different feather colors
Purely by where each one lives

flashcards.explanation_html: The two warblers look almost identical, so it was genetic differences and distinct songs that revealed them as separate species.

flashcards.back_html: A species that looks almost identical to another but is genetically distinct — often uncovered only with DNA, not by appearance.

flashcards.prompt: Why does this discovery matter beyond a single bird?

choices.text: It shows modern genetic tools keep uncovering hidden biodiversity
It proves all warblers are really one species
It means DNA testing is unreliable for classifying animals

flashcards.explanation_html: The find highlights how genetic tools reveal hidden diversity that look-alike species would otherwise hide.
